title: How to Stop Presenting in the Middle of Your Own Workshop
author: Workshopbank
summary: This facilitation-focused piece argues that experienced facilitators routinely drift from participatory facilitation into one-way presenting without noticing, because the drift feels productive from the inside, the room looks engaged even as it becomes passive. It offers five observable, physical warning signs, talking more than five minutes unbroken, nothing written on paper, being the only one standing, participants taking notes rather than producing outputs, and slides carrying answers instead of questions, precisely because internal instinct cannot be trusted to catch the drift in the moment. For each sign it pairs a specific verbal and physical intervention, arguing the fix must be physical before it can be cognitive, since you can't talk a room out of passivity. The essay's unifying thesis is that every fix does the same underlying thing: it takes the thinking work out of the facilitator's hands and puts it back in the participants'.
points: The core diagnostic insight, that presenter drift feels productive from the inside, with every internal signal suggesting things are going well, is what makes the five external, physical warning signs necessary rather than optional.
Each fix is deliberately embodied rather than verbal, such as having the group physically stand and move to dissolve the stage and audience dynamic created by one person standing at the front.
The distinction between notes and outputs, notes are a transcript of what you said, outputs are evidence of what they concluded, reframes a room that looks fully engaged as potentially still passive.
The piece's single-question slide test, does it hold an answer or a question, offers a fast, concrete audit for whether a deck is doing participants' thinking for them.
quotes: It catches experienced facilitators because it feels productive from the inside. You're explaining something, the room is nodding, and every signal you get says this is going well.

Five minutes is the ceiling. If you've been speaking for five minutes and the group hasn't done anything, you're presenting, whatever you planned to be. The trouble is you won't notice five minutes passing. It feels like two.
Notes are a transcript of what you said. Outputs are evidence of what they concluded. Only one of those changes anything on Monday.
If you're on your feet at the front and everyone is seated facing you, the room has become a stage and audience. Physical setup tells the group who is meant to perform and who is meant to receive.

There's a fast test for any slide. Does it hold an answer or a question? Answers are presentation slides. Questions are facilitation slides. Most decks run about eighty per cent answers, which means most of the slides are doing the thinking the participants should be doing.
The reversal is always physical first, because you can't talk a room out of passivity. You can only hand them something to do that makes being passive impossible.
